messages.subject: lm.rrpp anova or pillai's trace?
parts:
Dear colleagues,

when analyzing my data, I keep wondering whether running anova or pillai's trace is the better method to extract the effect sizes and p-values for main treatment effects. In this paper ( https://github.com/WyattSP/Evidence-of-Parallel-Evolution-in-the-Dental-Elements-of-Sweetognathus-Conodonts/blob/master/Publication%20RSPB%20Code.R ) they use Pillai's trace, but in the original RRPP package, anova is the recommended method to derive p-values from F-tests.

Which method do you recommend and why?

Thank you for your time!

Cheers
Bob

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] lm.rrpp anova or pillai's trace?
parts:
Bob,

There really is no solid right or wrong answer for which statistic to use, and one can include the Hotelling-Lawly trace, Wilks’ lambda, and Roy’s maximum root among considerations, also.  The only recommendation I would make is it depends on what you are testing and what kind of data you have.

The ANOVA-like statistics for multivariate data are based on traces of sums of squares and and cross-product (SSCP) matrices.  Since the trace of an SSCP is the sum of variable SS, these F-stats are one type of multivariate generalization that focuses purely on the amount of dispersion, explained and unexplained, but does not focus on the covariances among variables. By contrast, all of the multivariate coefficients are statistics that can be solved from determinants of SSCP matrices.  The trace and determinant are exactly the same for univariate data, but only then.  Determinants take into account variable covariances, become ill-conditioned when there are many variables, and become singular when there are too many variables (more variables than the number of observations minus the number of model parameters).  At this point one must do something ad hoc, like a data reduction method or penalized likelihood/matrix regularization approach.  We could spend a lot of time debating whether these ad hoc approach are preferable or inferior to using ANOVA-like statistics, which are not affected by the number of variables, but do not account for variable covariances.

So which is preferred?  How many variables do you have?  Are you testing differences among groups or associations between continuous variables?  Are you interested in locations of estimates in your data space or how correlated your response variables are, or both?  Are you merely groping for significance from a small P-value?  Or are you interested in effect sizes?

I am not interested in the answers to these questions for your data — just pointing out that the multifarious considerations preclude a simple answer.  However, there are two important things to realize.  First, in using RRPP, all of these are merely different statistics to use for the same process.  One could obtain P-values from SS, MS, F, R^2, Cohen's f^2, Pillai trace, Roy’s root. Wilks’ lambda, and Hotelling-Lawley trace, but they would do so for the exact same 1,000, 5,000, or 10,000 random permutations of residuals.  In doing so, if some are “significant” and this is what you seek, but some are not, then your effect sizes are probably not that exciting, regardless of the statistic you use or what you deem to be significant.  If they all consistently deliver similar large effect sizes, then take your pick.  Second, probably a more profound thing to consider is the type of SSCP you are estimating.  Types I, II, and III can produce quite different results and probably more diverse results than switching among statistics.  

For what it is worth, in my experience, if the number of observations >> the number of variables, borderline results with ANOVA-like statistics tend to be more significant with MANOVA statistics, due to the inclusion of variable covariances in the calculation of the determinants of SSCP matrices.  But I would never advocate for "gives me better p-values" as a reason for choosing one method over another.

Cheers!
Mike
